📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just a reminder that this sale runs until December 2nd, so you've still got plenty of time if you're after a bargain but can't bear the thought of the Black Friday crowds.
  • With Nintendo launching its Black Friday sale on the European eShop earlier this week, we knew it was only a matter of time before our friends in North America got some savings of their own.
  • Industry observers note that nintendo's 'Adventure Awaits' sale is now live on the North American storefront, with discounts across a bunch of first- and third-party delights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just a reminder that this sale runs until December 2nd, so you've still got plenty of time if you're after a bargain but can't bear the thought of the Black Friday crowds. Carry on!

With Nintendo launching its Black Friday sale on the European eShop earlier this week, we knew it was only a matter of time before our friends in North America got some savings of their own. And what do you know, they have!

Industry observers note that nintendo's 'Adventure Awaits' sale is now live on the North American storefront, with discounts across a bunch of first- and third-party delights. It'll be sticking around until 2nd December at 11:59pm PT, so you still have a couple of weeks to make the most of it.

Just like with the EU sale, we have assembled the following list of every game in the Adventure Awaits offer that we awarded a 9/10 or higher. We've also added a personal pick from the 8/10s at the end, because we couldn't see it go unmentioned.

As ever, if you're looking to grab some eShop credit before diving in, we've got you covered with the following links from our store.

According to recent reports, please note that some external links on this page are affiliate links, which means if you click them and make a purchase we may receive a small percentage of the sale. Please read our FTC Disclosure for more information.

13 Sentinels: Aegis Rim is a wonderful achievement for dynamic storytelling, as it puts forth a compelling and multifaceted narrative that’ll keep you guessing right up until the very end.

Sources indicate that this excellent story, combined with enjoyable combat portions, a striking art style, and some top-notch voice acting make for an experience that you shouldn't miss. It’s the kind of game that’ll have you wishing that you could play it again for the first time, just so all its best elements could be new again.

Aegis Defenders is a fantastic game, brilliantly blending the tower defence and platforming genres in a unique way to produce a memorable and enjoyable experience.

Lovable characters, interesting lore, plenty of secrets, engaging gameplay, and gorgeous presentation combine to make this a must-have for your Switch, a real gem on the eShop.

AI: The Somnium Files – nirvanA Initiative is one of the most interesting visual novels we’ve played through in a while. The murder mystery at its heart is brought to life by some great writing and quirky characters alongside the satisfyingly integrated, beautifully balanced Psync puzzle elements.

Even with some minor control issues, there is a lot to love in this game, even if you never picked up the original. Highly recommended if you're even a little bit curious.

The Nintendo eShop would be a considerably more exciting and interesting place if it were packed full of games like Ape Out. It’s a refreshingly original experience that more than deserves a place in any Switch owner’s library.

Difficult, frenetic gameplay, strong art direction, and an even stronger jazz drum soundtrack make this the sort of memorable game that you’ll likely keep coming back to over and over for another few runs in arcade mode. Ape Out gets a strong recommendation to anyone looking for a distinct and unforgettable game for their Switch collection; it’s a bit of an acquired taste, but well worth your time.

BALL x PIT is a tremendous brew of so many ideas it ought to collapse under the confusion. However, it operates in such perfect balance that it appeals both to the one-more-go instinct and to more cerebral planning and creativity. Kenny Sun Studios set itself a heck of a challenge but, fortunately, hasn’t dropped the ball.

It's out on Switch 2, too - and the upgrade is free.

Industry observers note that card Shark is the kind of game that at first blush seems like it just won’t work. Lots of dialogue bookended by brief, simplistic minigame sequences seems like it would make for an experience that would lose its lustre swiftly, yet we couldn’t put it down.

Recent findings suggest that witty writing, high-stakes gameplay, and a gorgeous art style all come together here to make for a game that’s well-executed and unique in its appeal. If you’re looking to try something awesome that notably bucks most modern gaming trends, Card Shark is absolutely something we’d recommend, well worth your time and money.

Catherine: Full Body is a fantastic revamp of a bona fide cult classic. With an excellent latest character and several new endings slickly inserted into an already highly entertaining narrative – not to mention a slew of fun new modes – this is the definitive version of an outstanding game.

If you've never played Catherine before, then you're in for an absolute treat, and if you have, we'd say there's enough new content here to make it worth diving in all over again.

It has been revealed that an extremely impressive first game from The Wild Gentlemen, Chicken Police - Paint it RED! is one of the best visual novel/adventure games we've played in a long, long time and one hell of an absorbing tale. It looks and runs great on the Switch, with only a couple of really minuscule interface issues which are easily ignored.

At roughly eight or nine hours, the story is surprisingly lengthy, but we were never bored and wanted to investigate every little thing just to wring out more precious droplets of banter and fascination. Chicken Police is a polished, captivating experience and we're very excited for whatever's coming next from this team.

According to recent reports, it's difficult to get across exactly why Danganronpa V3: Killing Harmony is so good without spoiling vast swathes of it, so we'll keep it simple. You'll come into the game baffled as to what the writers were thinking with some of these characters, and walk away loving each and every one of them.

In a recent development, there isn't a single moment of slack throughout the whole 40-hour playtime, it has the most extensive post-game of any title in the series, and one of the best endings to any game ever made. Go in blind and we promise you'll be in for the ride of your life.

According to recent reports, dark Souls: Remastered is a faithful remaster of a touchstone in video game design that improves overall performance of the original release while preserving all of the character traits that made it such a memorable experience. While it’s no less forgiving — and its menus are a little fiddly — this slick Nintendo Switch iteration offers an excellent way to experience Lordran’s ultra-challenging odyssey in true handheld form.

According to recent reports, plus, there's a Solaire of Astora amiibo. Praise the Sun, indeed.

Recent findings suggest that this is an excellent port of a game that feels like it’s found a natural home on Switch thanks to a plethora of control options and the console’s natural facility with vertical orientation. Short of popping your 4K TV on its side, Switch offers the very best way to play Downwell.

Industry observers note that its roguelike structure and twitch platforming might not be for everyone, but you should really give it a chance. For our money, Downwell is a modern classic that should be in everyone’s collection; for the pocket change asking price, it's a steal.

Along with the expected multiplayer modes (ranked and casual battles), Faeria delivers a compulsive, interesting and frankly enormously fun card battle experience. While not the easiest game to explain, it's an impressive teaching tool for itself, but never feels overwrought or tiresome in noted education. Of the card games we've enjoyed on Switch, Faeria is easily the highlight of the bunch and deserves to do well. It's a full-featured package and stands out as an excellent card/board/strategy experience. If you want to play a fantasy card game on Switch, we'd recommend this one first.

Every now and then, a game comes along that captures our hearts and reminds us why we love the medium in the first place. Forager features wonderfully designed crafting mechanics, addictive progression systems and more charm than you can possibly handle. Although it has very minor drawbacks, there's enough good stuff present here for us to confidently recommend adding Forager to your collection.

Heretic + Hexen is yet another slam dunk for Nightdive Studios. This latest release revamps both titles with modern controls, bonus content, and thoughtful changes to the core design that make each game a delight to play.

Granted, these are still FPS titles from the mid-'90s, so your mileage will definitely vary, but for returning fans and those with a particular fondness for old-school 'boomer shooters', you really can't go wrong. Now let's get a native Switch 2 port with 120fps please, Nightdive.

In a recent development, invisible, Inc. is a brilliant little tactics game, right up there with Into the Breach and XCOM – if not even better. The bite-sized structure belies a deceptively complex and meaningful game, where all your decisions ultimately mean something significant for that final desperate attack.

If you enjoy stealth or tactics games – or you're simply looking for a way into either genre – then Invisible, Inc. deserves your attention.

In a cynical era where nostalgia is pumped for all its worth with endless soulless remasters, Katamari Damacy Reroll serves up an engaging and rewarding game that hasn’t let any of its original charm or personality be lost in the transition from one platform to another.

With support for gyro controls and multiplayer — not to mention a degree of performance that sees it run smoothly in both handheld and docked mode — this Switch edition is easily the best way to play it outside of blowing the dust off your old PS2.

Altogether now: Naa na-na na-naa na na na...

An absolute pleasure from start to finish, what Kaze and the Wild Masks lacks in originality it makes up for in the strength of its level design, responsive controls, kinetic move set and attractive visuals. Excellent, action-packed platforming through and through, with great gameplay variety and gimmicks that don’t compromise on what the game is best at — challenging, fast-paced obstacle courses and deviously hidden secret areas.

Easiest sell? Kaze and the Wild Masks is to Donkey Kong Country what Freedom Planet was to Sonic the Hedgehog. Don’t miss this one.

Kirby and the Forgotten Land is a great big colourful joyride of an adventure for our little pink pal.

This first fully three-dimensional mainline entry in the franchise is bursting at the seams with fun and inventiveness, managing to transpose everything we know and love about past Kirby games to this all-newly introduced arena whilst adding plenty of delightful new aspects as it goes.

Mouthful Mode is daftly entertaining, each and every level is packed full of secrets and dripping in wonderful detail, and there are enough side activities, collectibles, and co-op fun here to keep you entertained and coming back for more for a good long while.

Whether you're playing on Switch 1 or via the excellent Star-Crossed World expansion on Switch 2 (with upgraded visuals and 60fps performance to boot), this comes highly recommended if you're looking for a fun platformer to play with kids.

Kirby and the Forgotten Land - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Star-Crossed World (say that five times, etc.) gives you the base game at a delicious 60fps with a whole significant bunch of fresh content thrown in for good measure.

If you've had your fill of Forgotten Land on Switch 1, there's nothing here to warrant replaying the entire game again, but the 12 remixed areas that make up the DLC are uniformly delightful, the upcoming transformations are excellent, and there's even new challenges for hardcore Kirby fans to get stuck into.

Industry observers note that one of the best games on Switch and one of our favourite 3D platformers in years, polished to a sparkly sheen and packing some meaningful fresh content? That's a very easy recommendation and a truly excellent addition to the Switch 2's early lineup.

Sources indicate that mark of the Ninja: Remastered is an utterly stellar stealth game and it’s lost none of the magic that made the original such a critical darling. Strong art direction, an engaging story, well-paced open gameplay, and a slew of extra content all combine to make for a near-flawless experience that you certainly won’t want to miss out on.

We’d give this game a high recommendation to all Switch owners; it’s the best stealth game money can buy in the Switch library, and one of the best ones in any console library.

Metroid Dread was a triumphant return for both Samus Aran and developer MercurySteam. This is a hugely entertaining and exquisitely designed entry that was slicker than anything we've seen from the series so far.

With a bunch of fantastic fresh abilities, super tense and enjoyable stealth sections, plenty of great major boss fights, and a story that long-time fans will definitely enjoy, we can't really see how this one could have been improved. Pixel nostalgia and genre impact aside, there's a very strong argument that 2D Metroid has never been better.

Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom is a tremendous accomplishment. It’s a gorgeous-looking game with a fantastic soundtrack and does its spiritual predecessors proud by nailing the Wonder Boy mechanics while still offering something that will appeal to modern audiences. As long as you can appreciate that it’s still very much an old-school game at heart and you’re going to get some 8-bit era platforming trickiness as a result, you’re going to thoroughly enjoy playing through this adventure for the 12-15 hours it’ll take you to beat it. It may not be Wonder Boy by name, but it’s definitely wonderful by nature.

  • Industry observers note that the stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

Industry observers note that the stream showed off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Industry observers note that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

Industry observers note that as the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of significant ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more promptly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

Industry observers note that "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs remarked, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It took Battlefield Studios over four months to tell Battlefield 6 players what they can actually expect from the game over the course of this year, in terms of content - but we’re glad to see a proposal laid out nonetheless.

The developer unveiled a grand 2026 roadmap, covering three more seasons currently in the works, and a wealth of fresh additions across the entire game, including new maps and the introduction of a new theatre of combat.

In a wide-ranging new video dubbed The Year Ahead, members of the Battlefield 6 development team have revealed a lot of new information about the future of the multiplayer shooter, going over plenty of the features and new content coming over the course of this year.

The video confirmed that BF6 has at least three other seasons in the works. Season 3, which begins in May, will be followed by Season 4, and Season 5 later in the year. Season 5 is the most mysterious, which is understandable.

In a recent development, we’ve known about some of what’s coming in Season 3, such as the remake of Golmud Railway (now called Railway to Golmud), but the video also revealed that a remake of Battlefield 3’s Grand Bazaar - now Cairo Bazaar - will also arrive later in the same season. Other exciting additions, such as battle royale solos and ranked play for Redsec are also on the agenda for Season 3.

It has been revealed that season 4, set for July, looks to be the biggest so far, with the introduction of naval combat, which will be available across two maps. Tsuru Reef, which is said to be even larger than Golmud, the largest map in BF6. The Pacific-set map won’t be the only one, as later in the season, another remake will arrive, this time of the iconic Wake Island.

It has been revealed that the introduction of naval combat will bring with it a upcoming dynamic wave system, aircraft carriers with operational flight decks, and new naval vehicles. Custom lobbies and Spectator Mode are also planned for Season 4.

Season 5 will bring three maps to BF6, rather than two, but all of its content remains under wraps.

Perhaps a sour note is that almost all of the maps referenced and shown in the video are remakes of maps from other Battlefield games, or reimagined at the very least. The Battlefield series is no stranger to remaking its own maps, but Battlefield 6 appears to be leaning on it much more than past entries.

If it’s any consolation, however, the map remakes we’ve played so far in Battlefield 6 have gone through major changes that have contributed to giving them a different flow and feel from their classic versions, or even remakes in other BF games.

Over the course of 2026, you can also expect the return of persistent servers, as well as a server browser to find them all - just like the good ol’ days. This includes the ability to host your own, though it’s unclear quite how this is going to work.

Season 3 is set to revealed in the coming days, so you’ll be hearing back from BF Studios in the near future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs.
  • It has been revealed that in an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend.
  • Recent findings suggest that these comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ryan Cohen, CEO of GameStop - the self-proclaimed "world's largest retail gaming and trade-in destination" - is not happy with the emerging trend of games releasing without discs. Per the CEO, the industry's move away from physical games and towards a digital-only future is harmful to both consumers and businesses.

It has been revealed that in an interview with Bloomberg, Cohen explained: "When you buy a game, you should be able to sell it, trade it or lend it to a friend. Unquestionably, the decision to move to all digital has hurt consumers, and it’s also hurt GameStop.".

Recent findings suggest that these comments come in the wake of GTA 6's launch. The game, expected to be the biggest video game launch of all time, is not shipping on discs at all. Even if you purchase a physical copy of the game, what you will actually take home is a 'code in a box' - giving you a code you can redeem on your console of choice that entitles you to a digital version of the game. GTA 6 is not the first game to do this, but it is the most high-profile. Similarly to discs, codes are also region-locked (at least on the PS5), meaning that the proliferation of codes as a format isn't even helping make games more readily available in certain markets.

Cohen notes he's been in conversation with "the obvious [publishers]" but that he's had little sway on their looks. "Of course they don’t like [trade-ins] because removing a used copy eliminates an alternative to buying upcoming," he told Bloomberg. "They're taking away competition.".

Though Cohen doesn't name GTA 6 specifically in the Bloomberg interview, it's clear that he's talking about Rockstar's megaton launch (he explicitly tweeted "GTA. On a disc. In a case. On your shelf. Like if you still want a physical copy" two days ago). The lack of trade-in potential is clearly harming his business; the Bloomberg article reveals pre-owned and refurbished products make up 22% of the GameStop's sales, down 32 percent from the same time a year ago.

In a recent development, of course, the proliferation of game-in-a-box products doesn't end with GTA 6. Sony aims to stop producing physical discs for latest PlayStation games starting in January 2028, moving to a digital-only model despite pushback from consumers and certain developers and publishers. The outcry is doing little to influence Sony's decision, however.

In a recent development, disc or no disc, GTA 6 is expected to cross $2bn in its opening weekend, and at the moment that is looking like a conservative figure, too. It's estimated the game has sold well over 19.05m units at the time of writing. Despite the astronomical sales, though, employees at Rockstar are still worried about layoffs. Additionally, a tribunal between the studio and fired IWBG union members (who were fired for apparent breaches of their NDAs) just concluded, though the verdict may not arrive for many weeks or months.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#223942. Latest Update: How Nintendo Recovered After Stumbling In The Streetpass

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3072 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gameinformer ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How Nintendo Recovered After Stumbling In The Streetpass

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gameinformer

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By the time Nintendo ceased production of the 3DS in September 2020, the manufacturer’s last dedicated line of exclusively handheld video game devices had completed one of gaming’s most incredible comebacks.
  • Recent findings suggest that the move worked: In its first month at its new price, 3DS sales in America rose 260 percent.
  • Recent findings suggest that one obvious glitch with the launch was the games – or lack thereof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By the time Nintendo ceased production of the 3DS in September 2020, the manufacturer’s last dedicated line of exclusively handheld video game devices had completed one of gaming’s most incredible comebacks. But to come back, you must first fall, and fall the 3DS did soon after it first launched in February 2011: its first month-and-a-half sales numbers came in nearly 400,000 units short of Nintendo’s initial projections of 4 million units sold. Over the next three months, Nintendo sold just an additional 710,000 3DS units worldwide, with only 110,000 purchased in the United States. In response, Nintendo took drastic measures, slashing the 3DS price in America from $250 to $170 just a half-year after the handheld launched.

Recent findings suggest that the move worked: In its first month at its new price, 3DS sales in America rose 260 percent. According to metrics released by Nintendo last year, the 3DS family of devices ended its run at a stunning 76 million units sold, still half of the original DS’s total but far more than other Nintendo platforms like the GameCube (21.7 million), Nintendo 64 (32.9 million), SNES (49.1 million), and even the original NES (61.9 million). The little system that couldn’t eventually proved it could.

Recent findings suggest that one obvious glitch with the launch was the games – or lack thereof. Included in the modest North American 3DS launch lineup were just three Nintendo first-party titles: Nintendogs + Cats, Pilotwings Resort, and Steel Diver. Though a Zelda remake, a new Mario platformer, and a new Mario Kart would arrive by year’s end, traditional system-selling franchises were initially nowhere to be found. By the time the bigger games arrived, Nintendo’s three first-party launch titles were placed in the dustbin of history, something Game Informer predicted in its review of Steel Diver, which labeled the game as “destined to become a strange and forgotten footnote in the publisher’s history.”.

Recent findings suggest that every first-party launch title communicates, both intentionally and unintentionally, something about the system upon which it’s launching and the company that created it. Last year, for instance, Mario Kart World evidenced that seamless open-world design and an interest in making buckets of money would remain hallmarks of Nintendo’s Switch 2 era. So, what can these three largely forgotten launch games tell us about the 3DS and Nintendo more broadly?

It has been revealed that initial hardware reviews of the 3DS contained two recurring thoughts: The glasses-free 3D effect was impressive when it worked – but it didn’t always work. Engadget’s review further hypothesized that “a lot of people are going to buy a 3DS and find they don’t really care for the 3D effect.” By the time Super Mario 3D Land released nine months after launch, Game Informer’s Bryan Vore was startled to find he was using the system’s primary feature at all, writing, “What surprises me most about 3D Land is how well the 3D effect is handled. I kept the 3D slider up most of the game”.

Indeed, in Nintendo’s 2011 fiscal year report, president Satoru Iwata theorized that initial 3DS sales were underwhelming because the firm had not done a convincing enough job of explaining the system’s signature innovation to potential customers: “The value of 3D images without the need for special glasses is hard to be understood through the existing media. However, we have found that people cannot feel it just by trying out a device, rather, some might even misestimate it when experiencing the images in an improper fashion.” Just two and a half years after the system’s launch, Nintendo began selling a fully flattened version of the handheld, appropriately named the 2DS.

Part of the issue with the underwhelming launch was that the 3DS lineup lacked an obvious killer app: There was neither a clear game that made purchasing the handheld an easy decision, nor was there a game that immediately proved that the 3D effect was anything more than an optional gimmick. In fact, among the three first-party titles was a game that had been designed nearly to completion before the team even learned of the existence of the 3DS.

When Nintendo first began showing the original DS to journalists at E3 in 2004, included among upcoming releases, like Metroid Prime Hunters and WarioWare Touched!, was a humble submarine simulation tech demo. IGN’s hands-on preview called the sub demo “simple in concept, but surprisingly complex in its controls and gameplay,” noting that it was “one of those ‘fun, but not quite a full game’ games at Nintendo’s booth, so it’s hard to say if development teams will expand on Submarine’s design to make it a more complete package.” At first, the team that made the demo, comprising veterans from Star Fox and F-Zero, was also unsure if they would expand it into a full game, as many of its members began work on other projects like Wii Fit.

Industry observers note that much later, producer Tadashi Sugiyama said in an Iwata Asks interview posted on Nintendo’s website that Nintendo of America asked the team to reconvene and release the submarine demo as downloadable software for the Nintendo DSi. But as the game – soon to be titled Steel Diver – expanded from just one mode (the side-scrolling submarine exploration and combat that would form the bulk of the game’s missions) to three modes (including Periscope Strike, a first-person torpedo shooter from the perspective of a periscope, and Steel Commander, a top-down strategy game partially inspired by the Japanese-exclusive 1990 Game Boy game Kaisen Game: Radar Mission), the Steel Diver team – now composed of both Nintendo designers and the 11 members of Giles Goddard’s firm Vitei – decided to expand their demo into a full retail release. This initially led to an identity crisis for director Takaya Imamura, who revealed to Iwata that he briefly, “thought it would be fine to set the game in a flashy, glittery world like – and I’m not kidding – a submarine version of Mario Kart.” Sugiyama swiftly shut that idea down, and the game proceeded with more traditional aquatic environments.

Recent findings suggest that highly invested in the project was the legendary Shigeru Miyamoto, who held a key piece of information from the team: Though Steel Diver was developed for the DS, he thought that it would make an even better showcase for the company’s yet-to-be-revealed 3DS. But it wasn’t until very late into the development process that the Steel Diver team even learned of the existence of the newly introduced console, a decision Miyamoto explained in Iwata Asks: “I knew the game was perfect for the Nintendo 3DS system, but I was afraid that if we switched from the Nintendo DS system to the Nintendo 3DS system in the middle of development, the contents wouldn’t be thoroughly fine-tuned. So after the Nintendo DS version was about done, I said, ‘Let’s shift this over to the Nintendo 3DS system.’” According to Imamura, “[w]hen we heard that, we already had intends for debugging. Development was all but over.”.

Sources indicate that the process of adding an extra dimension to the game proved difficult at first, with Imamura telling Iwata, “We thought we could just switch it over and it would look stereoscopic, but when we did, we couldn’t see it. […] We were among the first to develop software for the Nintendo 3DS system, so a sufficient development kit didn’t exist at the time.” But then, “one day it suddenly started popping out,” Goddard said in that same Iwata Asks article. And it came at just the right time, Goddard added: “It started looking 3D about the day before our presentation. If it hadn’t, the whole thing might have ended.” Ultimately, Imamura felt that the game had found its correct home on the 3DS, even if the process could have been improved: “I’m really glad we changed it over to the Nintendo 3DS system. But I think it would have turned out even better if Miyamoto-san had told us sooner that he wanted to make it for the Nintendo 3DS system [laughs]!”.

In a recent development, when the Wii rolled out in 2006, it came bundled with a number of pre-installed “channels” – or what we would likely just call apps today. Among those was the Mii Channel, an avatar-maker co-directed by Animal Crossing and Splatoon creator Hisashi Nogami. In an Iwata Asks interview, Nogami noted that something like the Miis was an idea Miyamoto “had wanted to realize for some time.” Nogami revealed that originally the “plan was to develop three games in which the same characters designed by the player would appear.” But as development on the Wii advanced, the concept had “broadened to encompass the entire Wii.” Miis were integral features of the Wii’s user-interface, appearing in a large number of games including, most importantly, the Wii’s landmark pack-in, Wii Sports, and becoming a defining aspect of Nintendo’s cultural identity. In a 2008 fiscal report Q&A, Iwata made clear just how seriously the organization viewed Miis as part of its brand, stating that, to “Nintendo, licensing Mii is identical to licensing Mario.” The Mii was now Nintendo, and it should be treated like its other icons.

However, it was not immediately clear to the general public whether the Mii was tied specifically to the Wii – with which it shared all but one letter – or if it would become Nintendo’s default avatar-creation system for the next two decades-plus, as we now know it has. Having launched in 2004, the DS did not include native Mii creation software, but it demonstrated the first small signs that the Mii would become a core part of the larger Nintendo ecosystem.

In a recent development, first, the thrillingly titled DS exercise game Personal Trainer: Walking – released in 2008 in Japan and 2009 in America – tied players’ pedometer-tracked steps to Mii avatars, which could be imported over from the Wii’s Mii Channel. However, players who did not own a Wii could only choose Miis from a series of random presets; there was no way to create a custom Mii within the game itself. The first DS game to feature a full Mii creation suite was 2009’s Tomodachi Collection, a Japan-exclusive social simulation game that would receive a more widely released sequel on the 3DS in 2013/2014 (a third game will arrive later this year.) But only three other DS games featured Miis at all: Ide Yousuke’s Healthy Mahjong DSi, a Japan-exclusive downloadable mahjong game; Kuruma de DS, also exclusive to Japan, a GPS-connected title made in collaboration with Toyota and Honda that could only be used in select cars; and Final Fantasy Crystal Chronicles: Echoes of Time, which could feature a Mii-emblazoned item only if the player was connected to someone playing on a Wii.

It wasn’t until the 3DS that it became clear that Miis would truly migrate away from their home system. The 3DS was pre-installed with an avatar creation application called Mii Maker. One of the system’s novel features was “StreetPass,” a communication system that allowed players to exchange data with other nearby players. Its showcase app was StreetPass Mii Plaza, in which up to 10 Miis could congregate and compete in minigames. By the end of 2013, the 3DS even had its own version of Miiverse, the Mii-based social network that first appeared on the Wii U.

The surest sign that Miis were here for good was Pilotwings Resort. The 3DS launch title was the third – and final, for now – entry in the Miyamoto-created Pilotwings franchise of flight-simulation games. Each of the previous games had also served as North American launch titles for their respective systems, with each game functioning as a technical showcase for its system’s upgraded graphical capabilities. 1991’s Pilotwings utilized the Super Nintendo’s Mode 7 graphics to deliver groundbreaking “3D” visuals, while 1996’s Pilotwings 64 gave players the chance to explore the Nintendo 64’s more authentically three-dimensional spaces. Pilotwings Resort continued this trend, affording early 3DS adopters a massive playground to experiment with the system’s stereoscopic 3D visuals.

The earlier Pilotwings were not full of classic Nintendo iconography, but Pilotwings Resort represented a major aesthetic break: Every character in the game was a Mii. This aligned the game more closely with a different recent – and more recognizable – Nintendo series: Wii Sports. The action of Pilotwings Resort even takes place on Wuhu Island, the fictional tropical location where 2007’s Wii Fit and 2009’s Wii Sports Resort were also set.

The origins of the island, however, trace back even further. When Nintendo showcased the Wii to journalists in May 2006, Wii Sports contained an additional game that was cut from the final release: a flight simulator called Airplane, in which players soared above an unnamed island that bore a number of striking similarities to Wuhu. Interestingly, as detailed in a 2006 Eurogamer article, Nintendo reps were quick to downplay any connection between Wii Sports Airplane and the Pilotwings franchise, with Matthew Kumar writing, “It’s not a Pilotwings, they say, despite featuring a lovely, relaxing island which features small towns to buzz over, and tunnels to barnstorm. And, oh, you know, rings to fly through to get points.” Additionally, Kumar wrote, “It’s not entirely clear how this would fit into the Wii Sports range (or pack) or, despite what they say, if it is even intended to. But as a tech demo for that Pilotwings game they’re going to unveil at TGS or something, it’s brilliant and I’m gasping for more.” By the time Pilotwings Resort finally saw the light of day a half-decade later, the Wii Sports franchise – and its iconic Miis – had climbed so high up the hierarchy of Nintendo’s first-party franchises that IGN’s review of the game opened with, “Wii Sports Resort is back. Did you miss it?”.

Sources indicate that miis appeared throughout the 3DS’s lifetime. They served as player icons for games like Super Mario 3D Land and Kid Icarus: Uprising, even starring in their own idiosyncratic games like Tomodachi Life and Miitopia. Miis would also be baked into future systems like the Wii U, the Switch, and the Switch 2. But it was Pilotwings Resort – along with Mii Plaza – that demonstrated Nintendo had bigger and more serious aspirations for the Mii outside of the Wii.

When the original Game Boy introduced in 1989, arriving in tow was an accessory called the Game Link Cable. It allowed players to connect directly to other Game Boy systems, enabling competitive multiplayer sessions in early hits like Tetris. Seven years later, with the release of the first Pokémon games, the Game Link Cable found a upcoming calling, allowing players to not just compete, but also to swap their pocket monsters with other players in their communities. In her book Super Nintendo: How One Japanese Organization Helped the World Have Fun, Keza MacDonald argues that this marked a turning point for Nintendo: “Pokémon Red and Pokémon Blue’s emphasis on trading and sharing represented an inspired reinvention of the Game Boy Link Cable: Game Freak took a piece of technology that had been used exclusively for competition and made it about communication, as well.”.

That design principle – that games were about sharing and communication, too – reached its apotheosis with the 3DS’s StreetPass feature, which allowed the system to actively and, more interestingly, passively communicate with other nearby 3DSs via locally established, internet-free connections, even when the console was set to sleep mode. At launch, StreetPass was most prominently featured in the preinstalled Mii StreetPass Plaza app, which included the game Find Mii, an RPG in which players’ parties were filled with Miis taken from other 3DSs they had passed by. As producer Kouichi Kawamoto told Kotaku’s Stephen Totilo, Find Mii emerged “from our drive to make players feel like they accomplish something by using StreetPass”. It was an idle game powered by physical activity. In doing so, StreetPass’s communication had taken the sharing principles of the Game Link Cable in an entirely novel direction.

StreetPass was also implemented into Nintendogs + Cats, the best-selling of the 3DS’s first-party launch titles. While Pokémon players of yore had to establish a physical connection to see other players’ collections, StreetPass enabled Nintendogs players to passively interact with other owners and their pets. You could take your 3DS on a walk to an actual dog park, for example, and if there were any other 3DS owners in range, you would head home with a series of journal entries featuring their Miis, their pets, any messages they’d sent, and perhaps even a gift. These Miis and their pets would also soon begin to populate the game in other ways: You might run into them on a walk or even compete against them in dog highlights. Nintendogs on DS featured a similar feature – Bark Mode – but it required more active participation from players; with StreetPass, community-building was now a low-effort exercise (often involving actual exercise).

In a recent development, streetPass was central to Nintendo’s conception of the 3DS. In an Iwata Asks article, the eponymous Iwata said that the concept of the 3DS was, “Carry Around, Affect Each Other and Something New Every Day.” Nintendogs + Cats producer Hideki Konno further stated, “[W]hile it’s definitely okay to enjoy the game at home, I hope players will go out walking around with their Nintendo 3DS system as often as possible. There’s a lot for that purpose not just in Nintendogs + Cats, but built into the system itself”. StreetPass was exactly the kind of kooky invention upon which Nintendo made its name, and its legacy of encouraging players to explore the world lives on in mobile games like Pokémon Go.

It has been revealed that the 3DS would soon find better games – and better sales – but its modest launch lineup contained plenty of insight. Steel Diver’s winding path towards release evidenced Nintendo’s unwavering commitment to its internal ideas – and its most legendary designer’s unconventional style of communication. Pilotwings Resort further established a core part of Nintendo’s brand identity, while Nintendogs + Cats revealed that even the most straightforward of Nintendo sequels could still feature peculiar innovations. Stereoscopic 3D may not have been the future of gaming, but other elements of the 3DS have stayed with us forever.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim co-directed hit documentary You Can See Everything, which has done huge box office numbers on the 2026 movie schedule, does a very deep dive into Elizabeth Holmes after Theranos. Now, everyone from former employees to psychologists is weighing in on Holmes both before and after her fraud convictions led to a long prison sentence that she is currently serving in Texas. Recently, one of Holmes’ assistants, Aria Marinelli, from the early days of Theranos, appeared on the Assistants vs. Agents podcast and spoke about a few red flags she saw in her short time working for the disgraced CEO.

According to recent reports, marinelli worked for Holmes at Theranos in 2009, which lands right in the middle of the organization’s history, which was founded in 2003 and collapsed in 2016 before going completely out of business in 2018. Holmes went to prison in 2023. Marinelli wasn’t at the company long, by the sound of things, but did work directly for Holmes in her time with the Silicon Valley startup that promised big things with what we now know was a completely fraudulent blood-testing machine (a machine Marinelli claims she never even laid eyes on until seeing You Can See Everything).

In a recent development, in the interview, she highlights a few things that made her question whether she wanted to be part of the company and if what they were doing was legitimate. According to Marinelli, the suspicions started even before she accepted the job, as she explained:.

Sources indicate that I went and looked through old emails just to see if I was remembering correctly, and it turns out I was. So this is [an email to] a mentor of mine. I remarked: ‘It's looking like I have to get Theranos an answer tomorrow regarding their offer. It expires at COB, and they've already extended it once. I'm very hesitant to accept because the work and the work environment are really not my ideal next step. Something about it doesn't sit right, I guess.’.

She went on to explain that pretty early on, there was never a lot of talk about what the firm was trying to do with the machine. In typical Silicon Valley style, according to Marinelli, most of the talk was about stock shares, IPOs, and how much money they could all make. That was something else that didn’t sit right with her.

It has been revealed that not only did Marinelli never see the now-infamous device, but she never saw a blood testing lab at all and was worried that despite famous names on the board of directors, there seemed to be no one with medical knowledge. That also raised concerns for her, as she explained:.

According to recent reports, the biggest thing was that there was no lab. So I had noticed that there were no doctors on the board, and that's, again, been talked about ad nauseam, but I was willing to dismiss that as maybe they were just getting started, right? And I remember just being told, ‘Oh, it's off-site,’ but I never saw anybody in that time frame that was working in a lab or that was from that lab.

Sources indicate that the final straw for Marinelli was when she was tasked with tracking down one of the company’s machines from the Army, which was supposedly testing it. Through multiple emails and phone calls, she seemed to be a wild goose chase, with everyone pointing to other people, and no one knowing where the device actually was. Marinelli told host Warner Bailey:.

It has been revealed that everyone [at Theranos] is very secretive, very, you know, shielded in how they're speaking about this thing. I doubt they would just ship it off to someone and not have them have a concerted program around testing it. So that, to me, was kind of the last flag that I was willing to put up with.

Marinelli also gave her honest impression of Holmes, and it wasn’t all negative, but she did mention that she thought The Dropout, the series starring Amanda Seyfried that can be seen with a Hulu subscription, is a fair portrayal of Holmes as Marinelli knew her. She also praised You Can See Everything and seems to have real sympathy for Holmes, saying, “everyone has to lie at that level.”.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sources indicate that one of the many interesting and brilliant things about You Can See Everything is that everyone sees something different in it, including the people who worked for Holmes and Theranos, and I don’t think this is the last time we’ll hear from people who worked with her and knew her. Especially as this movie continues to get Oscar buzz and will continue to be in the cultural zeitgeist for some time.

#223940. They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2473 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • According to recent reports, likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • Recent findings suggest that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

According to recent reports, likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

Recent findings suggest that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

Recent findings suggest that we'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

It has been revealed that that means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

Industry observers note that the problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a massive, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

Recent findings suggest that while we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I remarked, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

Sources indicate that I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of notable ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

It has been revealed that the "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

According to recent reports, for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

Industry observers note that all of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

In a recent development, if that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

In a recent development, indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

It has been revealed that both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

In a recent development, over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

According to recent reports, however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In a recent development, in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the latest PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Industry observers note that early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

Sources indicate that when it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint matter in bright ambient light.

If you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Industry observers note that not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

It has been revealed that the long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint issue. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Sources indicate that anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

According to recent reports, really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The substantial brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, presently, be entirely sure about that.

It has been revealed that second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The internet of today is a far cry from the days when Grand Theft Auto 5 was released, which is partly why Rockstar didn't bring back its own satirical version of the web in GTA 6.
  • It has been revealed that the web pages of Lifeinvadder, Bleeter, and Eyefind have instead given way to BuckMe, Scooter Bros, and WhatUp apps.
  • Recent findings suggest that "It didn't feel necessary for us," Rockstar North boss Rob Nelson told Kotaku.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The internet of today is a far cry from the days when Grand Theft Auto 5 was released, which is partly why Rockstar didn't bring back its own satirical version of the web in GTA 6.

It has been revealed that the web pages of Lifeinvadder, Bleeter, and Eyefind have instead given way to BuckMe, Scooter Bros, and WhatUp apps. The reason? Smartphone apps just made more sense.

Recent findings suggest that "It didn't feel necessary for us," Rockstar North boss Rob Nelson told Kotaku. "We definitely wanted to lean into apps and create these apps.".

Though some of the apps in GTA 6 perform similar tasks to the web of old, Nelson remarked the team didn't want players to be distracted from the game's detailed open world by staring at screens. That also extends to getting players to appreciate the value of money, and witnessing the progression of Jason and Lucia as they go from pawnshop robberies to staging major bank heists.

"They don't really need websites to be buying a lot of shit, you know what I mean, and so everything grows very organically," Nelson said, adding that websites may return in the future.

Sources indicate that "I remember asking Stu Petri, our head of 2D and UI, about websites, and he was like, 'For what? What do you need it for?' So, that was it," he added.

In materials supplied by Rockstar ahead of our review, Sam Grosset (associate UI director at the studio) also explained that a lot of thought went into how the apps work, and how easily the phone needed to fit into your play style in order for it to work as effectively as possible.

It has been revealed that "We ensure the UI feels like a natural extension of the game world, supporting players without interrupting gameplay or breaking immersion, unless necessary to do so," noted Grosset. "The UI should be complementary to the game and appropriate for each scenario. It was a big shift for our phone interface to be in-hand, but it supports that feeling of playing as Jason or Lucia and helps us stay embedded in the world.".

Rockstar would continually "raise the bar, question assumptions, explore new possibilities, and learn through rigorous testing and iteration" in order to make these apps - and the UX/UI in general - feel in line with the production quality of the rest of the game.

In Eurogamer's GTA 6 review, Chris Tapsell awarded the open-world crime game five stars, raving about its absurd level of detail, compelling characters, exciting action and of its big heart.

If you're looking to spend the next several days playing Rockstar's latest hit, Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough has detailed guides on everything from individual missions, to core mechanics like the new Wanted Level, and relationship and romance.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Diablo 4 is gearing up for its biggest post-launch event yet: the upcoming release of the Lord of Hatred expansion. As was the case with Vessel of Hatred before it, expansion releases alter the seasonal flow in a few ways, and Blizzard has now explained how.

The game’s next season - its 13th - has been officially revealed as Season of Reckoning. The new season will kick off alongside the expansion’s release next week, and will be available to all players, just like all previous seasons.

Although Season of Reckoning will roll out as normal, the season itself won’t be as meaty, at least when it comes to the sort of gameplay mechanics and themes players have come to expect from each upcoming season.

You’ll still find the normal Season Rank chase, Smoldering Ashes, and various rewards at each chapter. Season Blessings will also return, but that’s about it for progression outside of the game itself. If it’s any consolation, there are more goals and objectives to tackle this season.

Industry observers note that the even better news is that, according to Blizzard, future seasons will follow the classic format, which makes sense. The newly introduced season will come with a battle pass, of course, featuring four Reliquaries, as usual. The first Reliquary is free, while the others are paid.

Blizzard has also confirmed the the pre-load for Lord of Hatred is available now on all platforms. Even if you’re not getting the expansion, patch 3.0.0's pre-load includes all expansion content regardless, so you may as well pre-download it to be ready for April 27/28. On launch day, you’ll also need to download a smaller patch, version 3.0.1.

In case you missed it, we published our Lord of Hatred review earlier in the week. Give it a read if you’re curious about the expansion’s impact on the narrative, and how it changes core Diablo 4 gameplay.

A modder using AI to create The Last of Us Part 2 multiplayer that Naughty Dog never gave us claims Sony can't do much even if it wanted to shut it down.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Sony put the brakes on one such mod. YouTuber Speclizer unveiled their mod at the start of this year, but two months ago, they announced it was canceled after they received a cease and desist from Sony Interactive Entertainment. However, another has emerged in the form of Twelve Weeks (via IGN), with the developer releasing a mod earlier this week featuring 4v4 team battles.

The creator, Kellie, admitted on Twitter that AI was used in its development, saying, "Claude code was used for most of the project." However, they note that no AI artwork has been used, with the dev explaining she made the artwork herself.

Over on a YouTube video for the mod, the developer's account claims that Speclizer's mod was subject to a cease and desist because it was paywalled, but "mine is released already for free and in open source." However, even if the devs do receive a letter from Sony, it's claimed that "since people have the source code to the full mod already, there ain't much they can do even if they do shut me down.".

It has been revealed that naughty Dog was creating The Last of Us Online based on the second game for some time before it was canceled in 2023. Word out of the studio was very favorable, with its director, Vinit Agarwal, saying some who worked on it thought it was "the best multiplayer game they've ever played.".

Industry observers note that the Last of Us had a shockingly great multiplayer mode, strong enough to rival other substantial hitters of the Xbox 360 and PS3 generation. Who knows how the sequel's would've been, but with how much better the gameplay was in The Last of Us Part 2 was, I reckon it could've been great.

"We're not done with The Last of Us": Neil Druckmann confirms Naughty Dog has "a couple projects in the works," even if the TV show is ending.

#223935. Tech Report: Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

Tech Report: Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives.
  • Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria.
  • There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

There's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

It has been revealed that you lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

Industry observers note that the game's New York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

Back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's Fresh York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

💡 Key Takeaways
