📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, 1999's Thief Gold is widely considered the definitive incarnation of Thief: The Dark Project, adding three levels to the Looking Glass stealth sim while tidying up some bugs, but it has one grievous failing, in the eyes of many: the notorious Thieves Guild. In this all-new sixth mission, master catburglar Garrett must infiltrate the lair of a gang of pickpockets, after they filch a vase he had his eye on. The lair in question is actually very believable, as a hideout for criminals, in that it resists exploration even with a paper map. It consists of sunken, samey, obtusely arranged rooms that are made all the more headache-inducing by objectives that require a lot of backtracking.

In much the same way that I can admire a finely wrought pair of thumbscrews, I think the Thieves Guild is a clever creation, one that arguably shines when you use every ability or tactic in Garrett's possession rather than trying to ghost it. But it very easily becomes frustrating, to the point that many grizzled housebreakers advise new players to skip the level entirely. The Thieves Guild should be less frustrating in Nightdive's forthcoming Thief: The Dark Project Remastered, thanks to a more revealing spread of environmental textures and various other, furtive adjustments. As with many mods or remasters that speak of boosting the "immersion", I do worry that something valuable is being sacrificed in the process.

Sources indicate that in the course of a wide-ranging interview about how they're reworking this most devious of Dark Projects, Nightdive producer Daniel Grayshon explained that the map changes are "more in terms of background tech", than altering the fundamental design or introducing details that oblige different strategies. "They've gone into these levels in a sensible way to fix some practical problems with them, like some issues where you might be able to climb up to a place that you shouldn't have been able to climb up before," he commented.

Recent findings suggest that the Thief remaster team have taken more liberties, seemingly, with some of the Thief Gold maps. "Because some of the levels that were introduced in Thief Gold - they felt quite blocky and quite rushed, maybe, as you go through them," Grayshon explained. "But our team again, they've been able to go through and completely renovate some of these levels. The Opera House now feels in some parts like an actual Opera House, instead of a couple of blocky rooms. So I think players will really look at these and think, oh yeah, these kinds of details make sense, without it being too disruptive or too immersion breaking…".

In a recent development, "One particular - maybe people will consider infamous - level of the Gold package would be the Thieves Guild," Grayshon added. "The Thieves Guild is, if I were to sum it up kind of briefly, it is maybe two hours of walking through what feels like sewers, the same environment over and over again. There was no real visual distinction as to where you are in the level.

"So, we acknowledged pretty quickly that we need to go in and look at the Thieves Guild and fix it up, and what we've been able to do is texture it a lot more effectively. Give areas distinct looks, without compromising any of the gameplay again, like I mentioned. So we've put a bit more signposting around as well. Nothing that's going to be intrusive or immersion breaking again. Just kind of pointing the player in the right direction, as well as some other little things that I'm not going to spoil too much, but I think players will maybe appreciate the effort that we've done for this one.".

In general, Nightdive's broad aim has been "bringing those Gold levels up to the quality of the original and then taking all of those levels and then bumping them up to the next level - almost Thief 2 levels of quality in its environment design, especially in some of the mansions, and some of the later levels," Grayshon stated. "That's the level we were aiming for.".

Sources indicate that I have Several Thoughts about Grayshon's thoughts above (yes, people who dislike huffy armchair theory, this is your cue to skip to the comments). One is that I continue to dislike "immersion" as an ideal, though I recognise that many devs just use it as easy shorthand for a bunch of ways of doing art, sound and interface design. I think it often translates to uninvestigated enthusiasm for photorealistic fidelity and experiences that feel "smooth" and "engaging" enough to induce a kind of chemical trance. Many of the games I consider most valuable are cranky and unwilling and jarring, requiring you to think critically about the simulation rather than 'losing yourself' inside it. As regards the original Thief specifically, I enjoy how its nigh-magical stealth induces feelings of wavering dissociation, and keeps me guessing about the solidity of my own body.

In a recent development, secondly, there's the age-old argument that if you're going to preserve a game faithfully, you should preserve what it did badly. The Thieves Guild is a legend among players, much as Blighttown is among Dark Souls players and the Library is among fans of Halo: Combat Evolved. You learn much about the methodology of Thief at large from the guild's stifling contours, and it's thrilling to witness a bunch of very smart designers take a swing at a concept and not quite connect. I'll try to hold onto that rousing sentiment, when I'm playing the remaster and struggling to remember where they hid that damn vase.

CD Projekt made its Q3 2026 financial report today, and there's not a whole lot to see: The Witcher 3 remaster was a major hit, work on Cyberpunk 2 and The Witcher 4 is ticking along, and everyone really liked Cyberpunk: Edgerunners 2.

Perhaps understandably, a number of questions in the subsequent investors call put the focus on Grand Theft Auto 6. While CD Projekt joint CEO Michał Nowakowski didn't go too deep on the topic, he did say that the upcoming Witcher 4 will be comparable to GTA 6 in at least one way.

"Obviously, this is a call about us, not about Rockstar, but I do understand the connection here," Nowakowski said when asked if The Witcher 4 will represent a technological leap over its predecessor comparable to GTA 6. "Having said that, of course, I'm not going to make a deep dive and a full-blown review of GTA 5 versus GTA 6. But of course, we did look at the game. We did see the differences.

It has been revealed that "Do we believe there's going to be a comparable leap between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4? I think so, yes. I mean, it's been 11 years. We are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game. So yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4.".

Well, sure. As Nowakowski said, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt was released 11 years ago, and it'll be two more years before The Witcher 4 comes out—assuming it's not delayed, which would make it a rarity among CD Projekt games. It will also be the same number of years between Witcher 3 and 4 as spanned GTA 5 and 6. In the world of technology, 13 years is a long time.

Hell, just the upgrade from the original Witcher 3 to the remastered version that dropped earlier this year is notable:.

At the same time, Nowakowski stated that while the GTA 6 launch was tremendously successful, CD Projekt Red doesn't intend to merely mimic Rockstar's approach when The Witcher 4 is ready to go: "Our games are different and the require a certain different approach, and we just do certain things differently than they do.".

He also mentioned that while the release of GTA 6 has had an impact on Witcher 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 sales on consoles, he doesn't expect it to have a "material impact" on the firm's Q4 finances for one obvious reason.

"You do have to remember that a lot of our players are also PC-based," Nowakowski said. "GTA has not released on PC. We have not seen any impact whatsoever on the PC sales on engagement." And, he added, "on the PS5 and Xbox, it's not like our sales came to zero.".

Nowakowsi also mentioned that GTA 6 hasn't changed CD Projekt's ambitions for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2: If anything, it's "an inspiration in many ways for our developers." And he's not concerned about its success pushing up development budgets, because CD Projekt's games "are not budget-driven developments.".

Sources indicate that "I'm not saying that we don't care about the budgets. We do, and I'm pretty sure [Rockstar] did as well," Nowakowski said. "But you cannot make games like that having in mind, 'This is the fixed number of money I want to spend, and that's it. Otherwise, we're gone.'.

It has been revealed that "They are ambition-driven developments and money is key. The budgets are not indefinite. That's not what we're saying. But the philosophy is kind of like I said. And honestly, that philosophy has not changed for us because of GTA 6's release. It has just always been like that.".

Nowakowski's positive take on GTA 6 isn't too far off that of Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski, who said yesterday that he's suffering from "GTA 6-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression," although he promptly clarified that CD Projekt is "doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor." (And that he wasn't being serious about cancelling Cyberpunk 2.).

seriously though i think we're doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor. GTA is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed.

The Witcher 4 is currently slated for launch sometime in 2028, while Cyberpunk 2 isn't expected out before 2030.
